items.title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
items.author: Jennifer Ouellette
items.content: The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant. That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists. As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of "dry hopping" (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon. items.title: The Pragmatic Engineer Essay Challenge: Category Winners (Part 1)
items.author: Gergely Orosz
items.content: Before we start, a Black Friday special. With Black Friday coming up, you can get 20% off the full subscription for the first year - which is $120 for the year, or $10/month. Paid subscribers get access to full deepdives, The Pulse on Thursdays, to resources for engineering managers and software engineers, and to the full archive. Get this special offer The offer is available until Tuesday, 1 December. You can also gift this offer. To mark The Pragmatic Engineer’s fifth birthday in September, I launched an essay competition on the theme of how things have changed in building software since the emergence of AI models that are better than ever at coding. Engineers shared their experiences and observations, and a $10,000 grand cash prize for our favorite entry went to ‘How software engineering changed: a tale of two eras’ by Neil Kakkar. There were also six category winners who each won $2,500 in prizes, and in this article we’re happy to share excerpts from the winners and runners-up in three of those categories, also linking to 40 more articles. These essays by hands-on engineers and engineering leaders impressed us with their details of hard-earned experience, and are refreshingly honest and raw. Thanks to everyone who entered the competition and congratulations to the winners. Today, we check out essays on three different areas: What happens when AI writes all the code? How engineering practices have dramatically changed at startups and mid-sized tech companies in the twelve months since Opus 4.5 was released. The winner is ‘An engineering manager’s crazy year’ by Anton Zaides. Stories from solo builders. How one-person businesses and side projects that turn “AI-native” are building more, faster, and with higher quality. The winning essay is ‘I’m a 100x engineer now!’ by David Veszelovszki. Reflections on AI. What does this change mean for us human engineers? Thoughtful reflections which conclude that while agents can (and do!) write the code, engineers need to understand it to stay in control of systems and shape them. The winning piece is ‘The new core skills: agentic engineering at Granola’ by Jacob Bartlett. 1. What happens when AI writes all the code? At the end of 2025, many of us in tech saw AI’s coding capability dramatically improve with Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2, and the models suddenly become good enough to reliably write most of the code – and soon, almost all of it. In January, I asked: when AI writes almost all the code, what happens to software engineering? All the entries in this category covered the new challenges of AI generating the code, and how practices at many tech companies have adapted. Many writers compare a “before” and “after” with data on PR rates, revert rates, build times, and more. Winner: ‘An engineering manager’s crazy year’ Edited excerpt from the essay by author of manager.dev, Engineering Manager at HoneyBook: “It’s June 2026; a nice, sunny day outside when I sit at my computer, looking at a 10k-line PR opened by my team’s great designer, and I want to die inside. It’s not a mock or a prototype; it’s code he wants to merge into production. Not only is it full of hacky solutions (not even talking about criminal useEffect abuses), it also has dummy data where backend calls were supposed to be. How the hell did I get here? Let’s back up a bit. I joined HoneyBook as an Engineering Manager in October 2025. It’s a 13-year-old startup (raised ~$500M), a management platform for business owners (think CRM+contracts+admin, etc.). I joined to lead an existing team of seven experienced engineers responsible for the financial products like managing business expenses, loans, etc. This past year has been a crazy ride, going in just a few months from classic engineering to pure vibe coding, ending with the launch of a real zero-to-one initiative at an established company. Code review collapse We split our work into three repositories: the shared ai-workflows codebase, our own backend repo, and a thin frontend layer called atlas-vibe. Each had a different code review approach: In AI-workflows, every PR was thoroughly reviewed by at least two people including the engineer who wrote the code. In atlas-vibe, there were barely any PRs. We vibe code on the frontend, slowly improving the skills in our repo, and reducing the amount of substandard code a bit. In the backend repo, we had optional code reviews. That’s an interesting one. Slowly, it became more and more tempting to just not ask for reviews. It’s addicting to just develop a feature and immediately have it in production. There’s no need to have an open end in your brain. But still, at that stage I didn’t accept an ‘I don’t know, Claude wrote it’ approach. Even if you don’t request a review from someone, it’s still your responsibility to read and understand it. You can’t let Claude make the decisions and ‘drive’ the work. Output rose like crazy: Source: Weave It took me a while to understand that the code review stage contains a lot of peer pressure. When you submit your code to someone, you feel responsible for understanding it better, and nobody likes getting tons of PR comments (senior engineers, least of all). But when you know that nobody will review it, it’s much easier to cut corners in your own understanding too. So, in the span of a couple of months, we dropped from two people reviewing and understanding the code, to zero! The result was what you’d expect: a buggy codebase full of duplications and non-optimal patterns. Hands-on engineering managers (without giving up on the people side) From last October until March this year, I averaged one PR a week. Currently, it’s 20+. But more importantly, the nature of those PRs has changed: in March-June, it was mainly small things and side features, but since then I’ve taken on some more serious work myself, and it keeps increasing: Output as normalized units of work for an expert engineer. It’s been going up. Source: Weave I know there’s a lot of hate for the demand to go back to being hands-on from EMs, and I really understand it: I believe that people need us more than ever, and EMs who code all day are usually much less effective managers. In May, when we started to work on MyCo, I felt I just had to understand what our new flow looked like, and what we can improve. I believe it’s almost impossible to do this from the outside. For example, a debate with my engineer about our reduced quality in which I couldn’t participate properly without seeing the output myself, and I experienced both the advantages and limitations of the new flow. As our careers change, I believe that to be a good EM there is absolutely no other way than to join the building activity. I strongly believe that today, I have found a balance that works for me. I got rid of a lot of tedious work, and I feel as “present” as a manager as always, but now 10x more productive in my hands-on work. On Tuesdays and Thursdays I work from home and there are no meetings, and I’m able to release multiple big features a day. I was able to ramp up my parallel sessions to around 6-8, from 2-3 to fix some bugs along the way.” Read the full essay by Anton, where he gets into how non-engineers started to ship production code, why the team ditched their home-grown agentic solution for Eve by Vercel, and what Anton thinks about the future of building with AI Read the full essay Runner-ups We really enjoyed these five runner-up essays in this category about the “before” and “after” of AI and how it has changed software engineering: Software engineers are becoming “machinists” who need to build their own tools: PostHog engineer Paul D’Ambra makes an interesting point in his essay: “Software engineers are turning into AI Engineers? No, we are turning into software machinists. Replacing handmade software with (increasingly) cheap, plentiful, machine-made software. Unlike tailors who handcraft each item, machinists build tooling and inspect samples and then produce in large numbers. Two predictions: continuous integration and review will change next we make tools for our workshop Okay, things have changed less for folks working on systems with critical safety requirements, or high performance systems where it is easy to cause an incident. But the majority of us now have a different job. It is no longer sufficient to pore over every line of code, following the practices of bespoke tailored software engineers. Now, we are software machinists.” Read the full essay for details on tooling PostHog built like their deep review agents, and further predictions on change coming to CI. Learning how to enjoy working with AI Kira Howe is a Staff Engineer at analytics company Seeq and has been in a situation many of us can relate to. In her own words: “At some point earlier this year, I realized I was not enjoying work the way I used to. I will admit that I was one of those software people who was very unimpressed by ChatGPT in the early days, and I found the hype and excitement around LLMs really insufferable back then. Once it became obvious that these tools were becoming essential to how I work and not going anywhere, I decided I had to either accept my AI-centric fate and learn how to use them well, or leave the industry. I’ve come to believe that being a software engineer but resisting the increasing spread of AI tooling and applications is futile, and a recipe for misery.” Read the full essay – titled ‘Enjoying software engineering in the age of AI’ – for details on how Kira came around to feeling good about working with AI, and how practices at her company for CI, observability, and tooling changed. Bootstrapped company becomes AI-native Marc-André Moreau is CTO at Devolutions, a bootstrapped Canadian company of 250 people that builds remote desktop management and IT operations software. He writes: “October 2025. Claude Sonnet 4.5 has just come out, and everyone at Devolutions is going through AI training from Mindstone. The message from the CEO is clear: we are taking all the necessary steps to make the company AI-native. Employees are offered a voluntary departure package if they don’t want to be a part of this new “Devolutions 2.0”. Those who stay need to be committed and go all-in on AI with the rest of us. Here is the story of the profound shift that happened at Devolutions, and how a major migration originally estimated at three years was completed in just one.” A migration that should have taken ~3 years, per platform, was completed in less than one for Windows and Linux. Other platforms look promising Read the full essay for data-driven details of a complex application with 1,500 screens, the internal hackathon that ended up producing 60 useful skills, and how the company’s AI spending grew to $2M per year. Sixteen things AI changed in 2026 Carlo Beschi is a Lead Agile Coach at Treatwell, which employs 700 staff, and he shared a long list of what’s changed because of AI at the company in his essay: Paying off tech debt: Doing a lot more migrations and upgrades, and breezing through them. Prototyping: everyone is prototyping – not with Figma, Lovable, or Google AI Studio, but with Claude Design The “80/20 rule:” This says that 80% of the work is easy to get done alone with AI, but people are needed for the final 20%. Roles are blurring: devs are working outside of their domains and PMs are writing more code Mourning the craft: many engineers are having a hard time accepting that AI is taking over what they love in their job: writing well-crafted code Read the full essay, ‘The Earth is not flat’, for all 16 changes. Writing code became cheaper, but everything else became harder Bruno Felix, CTO at the fully remote, 8-person AI visibility startup XEO360 writes: “The last year was one of the most intense periods of my career. We’re in a transition where the main activity of a software engineer is shifting from rowing (focusing on one thing at a time and producing good code) to steering (managing multiple workstreams, context switching all day, and exercising sound judgment throughout). That is mentally taxing, and at times at odds with the skills, and sometimes the identities, we’ve built over the years.” Read the full essay for plenty of data on commit volume, CI time, and how practices changed. Shout outs Below are some other essays sent in by readers that get into detail about how things have changed. ‘Rebuilding our Deterministic Tax Engine for an AI Native World’ by David Nisenbaum, Founding Engineer at Sphere, on how the company did it with agents. ‘A year of contrasts: how software engineering is changing at Pulumi’ by Levi Blackstone, Principal Software Engineer at Pulumi. Case studies of shipping features in days that used to take months, and how build systems and engineering practices have changed. ‘Gradually, then suddenly: from “learn to code” to “coding is solved”… and back again’ by Marcell Dietl, Tech Lead & Software Architect at Frontmark, on why non-functional requirements remain ones that humans make, and how engineering practices and hiring practices have changed. ‘What a small team with old code can do with AI (and what it can’t, yet)’ by engineering manager Ygor Cardoso, including interesting details on the extra work created for devs when non-engineers start to contribute code. AI transformed the work at Homie by Abdul Osman, Founding Engineer at Homie on how they rewrote the backend three times in a year, the move from IDEs to terminals, and how developer practices changed. The return of a software engineer. Victor Zhang studied software engineering in 2006, then moved to work in finance. In 2024, he returned to software engineering at a 50-person company to freshen it up in Python, using ChatGPT. He writes that 2026 “changed everything.” 10x what? by Krzysztof Maliszewski, Software Engineer at Coralogix. This is an interesting survey of 40 engineers at Coralogix – where half admit they’re addicted to agents! Survey of Coralogix engineers. Check out the full essay by Krzysztof Maliszewski 2. Essays by solo builders and tiny teams We were impressed by some stories from readers about how far a single dev or a team of just 2–4 people can get these days, with agents helping them build software more ambitious than ever. Winner: ‘I’m a 100x engineer now!’ Edited excerpt from David Veszelovszki’s essay, the creator of Cmdr: ‘a file manager from 2026, the spiritual successor of Total Commander,’ and former Sourcegraph software engineer Don’t stop rollin’: David works on his house while his agents build Cmdr ‘After 30+ years of coding the old-fashioned way, I’m extremely enthusiastic and about 100x faster with AI! It has changed my entire workflow, and my life. While I’m writing this, I’m painting the kids’ room. Claude helped select the paint and calculate the amount I needed. I made all the decisions, I own everything that happened, while Claude did the research and prepared the decisions for me. That’s also exactly how I work. Today, while I’m painting, Claude is fixing bugs, developing features, and preparing a release. I’m even considering getting a day job because I could run my current project, Cmdr, for an hour a day, with agents carrying the rest. What a time to be alive! Speed! Lines of code is far from a perfect metric to describe complexity but it’s easy to measure and it kinda correlates with complexity? So I’ll use it here. An older snapshot of Sourcegraph’s main repo is still available so I know that my average output on the days when I pushed code was 194 LoC/day between 2022–2025 when I worked there. That many sweaty, reviewed, production-ready code lines from my own little fingers—okay, with the help of GitHub Copilot. And these were my active workdays. So, my real average output was closer to 100 LoC per calendar day. In contrast, I started Cmdr 10 months ago, and it’s 1.4M LoC now, +800k lines of translations, docs, etc. It’s 1.4M lines of actual code, most of it production and the rest tests. That’s more than 4,500 LoC/day added on average, including weekends. Last 30 days? 12,000. It’s speeding up. Discount 33% to compensate for the AI bloat. Still, what, 60x faster than when I only used Copilot? And 80–100x faster than without AI. Plus, I run other projects too, including Prvw, mtp-rs, smb2, and gitstrata. Number of commits and languages used when building Cmdr. See the up-to-date graph But if you don’t like the LoC metric, that’s fair, so let me add: 1,674 changelog entries over 10 months, each delivering a piece of user value. Increased from ~40/month in Jan–Feb to 230–350/month by Aug–Oct. 12,003 commits (avg. ~55/workday, but increased from ~15/workday in Jan to ~160/workday in Oct, so about 10x!). 67 releases so far, 7–10 a month, so ~2/week. That’s all pretty nuts, isn’t it? A glimpse of how I work these days: Claude Code with Opus 5.5 medium in a terminal, a single 20x Max plan Few-liner prompts and no specs No skills Almost no rule files now No reading specs/plans. Manual QA at the end No code reviews Claude-maintained dev&prod infra Grasping 100% of the product level, 0% of the code level Enter Opus 5.5: Fixing bugs by the dozen On October 1, I gave Claude a dozen issues at once. It went like this: I told it pretty much: “Hey, I’m painting a room today. Could you find 10 smaller tickets to do on your own, with subagents, then merge and push it at the end, make CI happy.” Claude shipped it in a few hours and closed the tickets. Then I said: “Nice work! Please take 10 more.” It was delivered the same way. In the third round, it brought me 8–12 UI bugs as a single category. I made the initial decisions, and it knocked them off in a few hours. We then did a fourth round the same way. On 2026-10-01, I closed these 42 GitHub issues total. Note: this was all bug fixing and feature development that didn’t directly touch humans. When issues included UI copywriting, Claude always brought the new strings back to me and I took five minutes to edit them before shipping. Why I work so fast – and you probably can’t I know that at a multi-person org, you as a single engineer won’t contribute 10k lines of code per workday in a project because you need to coordinate with other people. You need to be somewhat careful, loop in some people on what you’re doing, build common mental models of the system, and maybe even review code. My advantage as a solo eng is that I don’t have any of that overhead. The dark side of AI-assisted coding is that it makes sleep relatively costly, and building at crazy speeds can be addictive for avid builders. Take care of yourself. High-level work Lately, I’m much more of a product person and company leader than a software engineer. When I tell people what I do, I still say “I code” out of habit, but do I really? Well, I don’t. Claude codes, debugs, automates processes, translates. It does all the dirty work. And I put all that time into strategy, product decisions, marketing, customer service. Which means caring about the user and the product. I aim to be an expert on the product itself. I know all the parts of the app, I know exactly what each part can do and why. Every button, every dialog. But I don’t know the code. Screenshot from the interface of Cmdr I built the S3 connect feature in two days while painting the room. 50k LoC, fully tested with seven providers. Displays transfer costs based on current list prices. How nice is that? Overall, I’m extremely, extremely glad and thankful to be alive at this time and to be able to work with this tooling! It’s incredibly rewarding. It’s an unbelievably nice feeling that I can turn the “100x engineer” advantage into delivering quality apps with care and respect. It’s just hard to choose to sleep, too.” Read the full essay by David, where he gets into how he uses automated checks and balances architecture work to keep the code in order. Read the full eassay Runner-ups Below are two essays that we all found to be very engaging reads in this category: Four-person company with no more handwritten PRs The founder of Heartbeat, a platform for running paid online communities, recounted the AI-related change at his business which generates $1M+ in monthly paid bookings. Mayhul Arora writes: “We spent a lot of this year upgrading our development environment and systems to the agentic era. But it’s unclear to me how much of that work is left to be done. I think there’s a good chance that the future of our team looks like 2-3 people maintaining the core agentic factory and software platform, while everyone else builds customer-facing features on top of that foundation. Maintaining the core agentic factory looks like optimizing core primitives such as data fetching patterns, CI, the design system, scheduled agents, dev environments, etc. This is the work that’s easiest to scale up with agents. Building customer-facing features are the engineers that are able to live in planning mode and consistently translate loosely-specified features into concrete technical implementations. People that have the patience to iterate alongside agents, the taste to make the right tradeoffs and the wisdom to know when the existing architecture needs to adapt.” Read the full essay for more on dev tooling, CI bottlenecks, and why the team spends more time in meetings. One developer turns trad IT department AI-native Joshua Warren has been a software developer since 1999, and joined paint manufacturer Blend Supply to modernize its development process, as the only human developer. He writes: “Blend Supply is a third-generation family company that has been on the forefront of the aerospace industry since 1946. The easiest way to understand what Blend does - think custom-mixed paint for everything from private jets to 737s and boats. Blend previously relied on agencies to build and support their website, and I believe that agentic software development is going to disrupt development agencies. Blend Supply’s leadership has given me a blank slate, the rare opportunity to build from the ground up whatever I feel is necessary to help Blend out-develop their competition [with AI-native approaches and workflows].” Read the full essay for fascinating details on how Joshua built a software factory inside of a ‘traditional’ company on top of the Oh My Pi harness, agents attending weekly status meetings with sales and customer support people, and deploying 50+ times per day versus once a month. Joshua’s essay is a reminder that massive disruption is happening in “traditional” industries where IT has long been a cost center. This story also suggests that development agencies might be in trouble: Blend Supply replaced several agencies with a single engineer to build out their software factory! Shout outs Below are some more entries from readers that we found interesting or inspiring in some way: ‘Sure-why-not-driven-development’ by Marius Maaland, CEO of three-person AI startup Drippa. Founded in January this year, the code has always been fully AI-generated. ‘Building Bencher in 2026: open source, bootstrapped, and agent-pilled.’ Staff software engineer Everett Pompeii builds Bencher, an open source continuous benchmarking platform on nights and weekends. I don’t miss coding. I missed building. Leslie Nguyen was formerly an engineering manager at Block, Uber, and Pinterest, and launched personal finance app Stridefly on her own. She documents the number of commits, tests, and lessons she’s learned along the way. Leslie Nguyen built Stridefly by herself, and with a team of agents More shoutouts: ‘I am the bottleneck. We are’ – by Bogdan Deaky, founder of Bluemind Software. Bogdan runs his business with a single employee while teaching at a university. He argues that requirements gathering and verifying software output are the limiting factors in what one person can build. ‘Two years of change: how AI reshaped software engineering at a small company.’ Michal Gutowski is the solo developer at smAily, a bootstrapped remote company building an app to record in-person meetings. LLMs write all the code there. ‘Great product engineering in the AI era.’ Anirudh Ravichandra is cofounder of GP-LP Match, a real estate matchmaker. It’s a bootstrapped company of five people with two engineers. He writes about the importance of choosing the right tools. ‘Building an in-browser massively multiplayer (MMO) trading card game (TCG): and doing it all alone’ by Elijah Lee, creator of BattlerLegacyTCG. Elijah quit his job to build this game late last year. He used Elixir on the backend – despite never using it before AI – and in this essay, he goes through the tech stack, agent workflow. He’s honest on how hard it is to build a full-fledged game. ‘Engineering with concept art.’ Caer Mistral Sanders, founder of content studio With Caer, explains how she builds software as a solo founder, including Wrot, a writing tool he used to publish her essay. It’s a curious approach of creating lots of custom approaches and even data formats like Codas (similar to Markdown). ‘How I vibe coded a best-in-class communication app for my nonverbal child.’ This is a sweet story by Product Owner and father Andrew Peterson who built a communication app for his son after finding that commercial devices cost $1,700+ and are made for adults. Inspiring! Wrot, the online writing tool Caer created to publish her essay. See it here 3. Reflections on AI What does it mean that AI now writes most – if not all – the code? The essays below tackle this question not with data, but on the basis of how authors feel about this change. Winner: ‘The new core skills: agentic engineering at Granola’ In his essay, Jacob Bartlett documents how each new major model release has altered his daily workflow – and things changed monthly! December 2025: GPT-5.2 and Opus 4.5 January 2026: No major releases February 2026: GPT-5.3 and Opus 4.6 March 2026: GPT-5.4 April 2026: GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7 May 2026: Opus 4.8 June 2026: Fable 5 (unleashed) July 2026: GPT-5.6 Sol, Opus 5, and Fable 5 (nerfed) August 2026: no major releases September 2026: GPT-6 Astra, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5 October 2026: no major releases This excerpt from Jacob’s essay details what happened in February: “Typically, I’ve gotten into minor trouble at work for attempting to have my cake and eat it; trying to make a name for myself via 20% projects, but stacking it inclusively rather than on top of my regular hours. It’s the same line that I’ve heard throughout my education and career: focus and stop getting distracted. But that was in the beforetimes. The Granola iOS app began life as a side project by Jonathan, one of our fullstack engineers, to find out if meetings-on-the-go had legs. It did! Tom, our mobile lead, was hired to take it to production. Like all good startups, Granola optimised for speed-of-validation to get it into the hands of customers ASAP. This got the quick validation that was needed, but left a slightly rushed architecture in its wake. The 11-month-old iOS codebase was simple enough that I could quickly stretch it across my cranial context window, and ripe for big architectural improvements. In short, this was my perfect playground: an Eden of low-hanging fruit which I was neurologically wired to pluck. Could I resist this temptation? No. Did that get me in lots of trouble at Granola? Also, no. Now I had access to pretty-good agents, and an environment with a relaxed attitude to token expenditure. I’d just learned to parallelise my work across multiple git checkouts, and I’d been honing my ability to define iOS verification steps. Tom and I, importantly, were in total agreement on the architectural destination we wanted to get to. I flexed my multi-agentic chops, indulging my best and worst impulses. And I was getting praised for it! I dropped a just-one-more-thing slide in the all-hands and introduced the Meeting Bar™, a UI element that lets users dismiss meetings, and navigate through the app, without stopping their current transcription. Our product manager lamented about being trapped on the meeting screen, and I offered both a shoulder to cry on and a solution: an agentic skunkworks that toiled away in a secondary terminal tab alongside my standard day job, while I bounced a few early iterations off our designer. The Meeting Bar was delivered in 20% time. Over time, I’ve become proficient at designing verification steps; planning work alongside my agents; and context switching. Now I can run multiple meaningful projects in parallel. Separate to product-market fit, this felt more like neurodivergence-company-technology fit.” Check out the full essay for a more detailed breakdown of how each model release has impacted Jacob’s workflow. He concludes: “While software engineering has been revolutionised, this doesn’t make engineering skills less valuable.” Read the full essay Runner-ups Here are four essays we particularly liked for the reflections they contain. How AI changes software engineering Daniel Silva is a Staff Software Engineer at fintech startup Coverflex. His grounded essay reflects on the massive change he saw and took part in over the last year, concluding: “It seems that AI is really here to stay. It has transformed engineering for the foreseeable future. There are clearly eras before and after AI got good enough, where it now permeates every aspect of the development process. I don’t think software engineering is doomed. I still think AI is a tool that requires human taste and ingenuity to make it work. We will most likely need more software engineers because more software is getting created than ever. Infinite problems in the world are waiting to be solved. Engineers need to keep up with the times and be open to new ways of working with tools very different from the past. This has happened before: more powerful IDEs were created, high-level languages were created, and magnetic tapes replaced punched cards… We can do this again, for sure.” Read the full essay for more thoughts about the importance of “putting in the reps” into AI usage, why Daniel sees hope for junior engineers, why he does not use AI to write down ideas, and more. Nothing has changed about what it means to be a software engineer Ben Cohen is a Software Engineer at Substack. But he never felt “home” in software engineering circles. Ben writes: “My name is Ben Cohen. I am a software engineer at Substack, the company whose software powers the blog you are reading this (hopefully prize-winning) essay on. I use the phrase “am a software engineer” quite intentionally, because software engineering has always been much more of an identity than a job for me. (...) Despite all of the above, I’ve never felt at home in many software engineering circles. You see, here’s my confession: I don’t really care about code. I’m a little convinced that the people who talk about “beautiful” code are lying, in the way that I also don’t really believe that the wine snobs are tasting dried apricot notes in their rieslings. I don’t have a favorite programming language and my favorite code editor is the one that’s already open.” He closes with a feeling that not much has changed: “Everything is, of course, different now. Different in the way that it was different when we stopped using punch cards, invented the compiler, started building websites, and switched to cloud infrastructure. But also, nothing has changed about what it means to be a software engineer. Large language models have forced us, for the first time, to answer the question: “Is it still software engineering if you don’t write the code?” To that, my answer is an emphatic yes.” Read the full essay for Ben’s full thoughts on how he sees this change, and why the story about a famous engineer charging $10,000 to know where to hit a machine with the hammer could be true for us software engineers. A new grad software engineer’s impressions Max Oliinyk is a 22-year-old Platform Engineer at F-Secure who spent 18 months at Hive Helsinki: a full-time, on-campus program where students learn by building software products in teams with no teachers. After a four-month internship at cybersecurity company F-Secure, he got hired fulltime. Max writes about his current working setup: “Right now, I manage Jira, code writing, PR creation, documentation and research all through Claude. The only place where I will probably always prefer to do things on my own is communication. No one will get offended by code written by AI, especially if it follows all the standards established in the team and has the right ideas behind it. Getting a lengthy blob of text in response to your message or review comment is considered not nice, even beyond the industry. It is fine if the message is something functional; it is not if you wanted to hear something humane back. So, my current stack is Claude Code, with a subscription provided by the company that gives access to all recent models. I add skills on top of it, including ones with team-specific context that help agents follow our conventions. I am genuinely not able to burn through the limits; I occasionally run out of the 5h limit a bit too early if I use too much thinking effort, a too-expensive model, or launch a dynamic workflow.” Read his full essay for more observations on what it’s like in the industry at this time for an early-career engineer. Hope for early-career software engineers Fawziyah A is a software engineer with five years of experience, working at fintech Imprint. She tackles the important topic of what AI means for junior engineers. In her words: “Despite worries that AI is de-skilling early career engineers, being empowered to work on so many more projects, and with so much more variety, has taught me way more about my company’s business problems, priorities, and systems design. Less experienced engineers who charge at those challenges head on have the opportunity to learn faster than was possible a year ago. That is what makes me so excited to be working at a place like Imprint and working in this industry now.” Read her full essay for more reflections on less interaction among devs, how domain experience is readily available with AI, and how the technology can be useful for learning faster. Shout outs How software engineering at Hinge has changed. Jacob Voytko, Staff Backend Engineer at Hinge on how prototyping, on-call incident response, internal tooling, and design, coding and review changed with AI agents. What AI mustn’t take from us, Jachym Dvorak, Machine Learning Engineer at Productboard on which parts of engineering practice should be protected as AI changes the work. Software engineering in the LLM funhouse. Robert Lopez, Software Engineer writes about how AI changed development at Quizlet and Stellic. He argues that teams should return to first principles and do things like plan together, say no to scope creep, and measure more. How checking the math I didn’t write is going. Data engineer Sia Seko reflects on how data engineering has changed, and how her team changed habits while adapting AI. Back to coding after AI. Vitor Louzada, currently Head of Data Science at Grover returned to coding after a decade of being a manager. In a world of clankers, be a connoisseur. Duncan MacQuarrie, Senior Software Engineer at Infracost reflects on the tension between AI adoption and the growing cost of AI. The times they are a-changin’: software engineering in the age of agents. Software engineer Emma Gaubert argues that the value of a software engineer was never limited to writing code. She makes the point that engineers should broaden into product, design and soft skills. On the impact of artificial intelligence on my job and engineering identity. Jakub Niemiec, Senior Mobile Engineer and Creator of Beanie (a coffee companion app) works with Flutter and shares the downsides of AI: draining code reviews, fewer junior engineers, and the end of language-specific expertise. He closes with a hope that exciting times are to come. 5 new types of failures in AI-native development. Carly Rector, software engineer and founder shares her experience leading 8 AI-native projects in the last two years. Building a ladder of love (and trust). Maanas Sathaye, Systems engineer at Sightly, on how he and the team start to trust agents to do larger and larger pieces of work. Outsource the Work, Not the Thinking. Sara Spagnoletto, Software Engineer at Google, working on Waze, gives an interesting peek of adopting AI in her day-to-day work, and how she opened 3x as many PRs after starting to use Antigravity more. The work is changing. Christina Martinez, DX engineer at Resend on how non-engineers can ship code, experimentation becoming more frequent, and how work feels like it’s getting out of balance. Claude, the new kid in town. Dave Kiss, Staff Community Engineer at Mux, on how Claude changed engineering at the company. Takeaways In this issue, we went through the experience of 40 tech professionals – working from small companies to large companies; from building side projects to production software used by massive numbers of customers. Despite the variety the stories stayed pretty much the same: everyone recalled the massive change in pace with Opus 4.5 or 4.6, and how they’ve faced new problems to solve with the amount of code generated, with non-engineers coding, and so on. When reflecting on this large change hitting our industry, many of the engineers were positive in how engineering basics remain important in building systems, and deciding what to build. It’s worth noting that we had a “no AI” writing rule for this competition. Even though we delegate more of our coding to AI – when the target of that output is a machine interpreting it –, we still value the human voice when writing to fellow humans. Thanks again to everyone who contributed an essay, and congratulations to the grand prize and category winners. In part two of this mini-series, we’ll present the other half category-winning essays, and additional essays worth reading.

items.title: Signal Moves to Block AI Agents
items.author: Thorin Klosowski
items.content: Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app. Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “Intelligent Screen Context,” while Apple refers to it as either “Onscreen Awareness” or “Visual Intelligence.” Apple now provides a way to block Siri AI’s access to apps, but by default every app is available to Siri AI, so it’s up to the user to go in and put these guardrails up. Signal requests that protection on your behalf. Google doesn’t currently offer any sort of similar option. So Signal on Android does the best it can, by turning off screenshots when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. Signal’s solution helps ensure that, unless you go in and change the setting yourself, it defaults to the most private option. While this is a clever solution to the current issues facing Signal (and potentially useful for any other app that does its best to promise privacy), we need all operating systems to provide stronger methods and clear documentation to developers so they can safeguard their users without needing to jump through hoops. Both developers and users should have the tools they need to safeguard their own data from AI agents and other AI tools. *Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

items.title: Back-to-back measles deaths is our new reality; US tally now at 14
items.author: Beth Mole
items.content: Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water. The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died. Deaths and transmission On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child. items.title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
items.author: John Timmer
items.content: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset. It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math. Tackling Riemann The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field." Read full article Comments

items.title: New York and California Age Gating Rules Go Into Effect in the New Year
items.author: Rindala Alajaji
items.content: Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027. EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users. What California’s Rules Say Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709. For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking. At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users. What New York’s Rules Say Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service. As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics. The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)). Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week. What This Means for Users in NY and CA Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today. When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current issues. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights. At the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine. Help Us Help You Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, New York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org. Take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts. If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

items.title: Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
items.author: Nick Indge
items.content: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide. Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote. The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident. items.title: Jensen Huang Reinstated As Nvidia CEO at Behest of President Trump
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: In the evening of November 22, Donald Trump said he ‘hoped’ the Nvidia board would rehire Jensen Huang, as the ‘best thing for the Company.’ Shortly after that Donald Trump called the Nvidia board. On the morning of November 23, Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia. Andrew Curran: President Trump live on CNBC [on Monday night]: ‘I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly.’ It was an excellent day for the stock market. Over three trillion dollars in value was added. Nvidia alone was up over 30% on the day. It was a tragic day in many other ways. This may go down as one of the greatest scandals in history. It was a dark day for our democracy and free market economy and the rule of law, and for the integrity of our government. This will forever, or at least for the next two years, factor into every decision made, and every trade in the stock market. It was the triumph of hostile action, of deliberately setting things up to collapse without you. In the era of Donald Trump, it was the ultimate ‘nothing matters’ moment. It likely means that Nvidia is going to go back to maximizing, in an adversarial way, how many chips it can sell to China, and to those who will smuggle into China. It also means that, as in the playbook of OpenAI’s Battle of the Board, the tech vibe army and its commanders are hard at work gloating, and trying to pillage, and to memory hole all of the things Jensen Huang did. They celebrate, emboldened now more than ever to play a hostile game where they make themselves impossible to fire by threatening to blow up their companies, including by threatening the scalps of anyone who dares oppose them. They are acting as if this was a hit job from The New York Times, rather than pointing out true and important facts about the world that others were also scrambling to report. They are calling that reporting a ‘failure’ because Jensen Huang is once again CEO of Nvidia. There are continued attempts to blame some cabal. These people work on vibes, so they think that because they ‘won’ they should therefore get rewarded in various ways. They will try to imply this means there shouldn’t be tightening or enforcement of export controls, and other such things. I hope and expect Congress to think otherwise, all the more so. This is far from over. The national security state is no doubt furious. There are going to be extensive Congressional investigations, and also extensive criminal investigations. Jensen Huang is scheduled for three House committees already. The reporting will continue. There is new reporting on many fronts. Table of Contents I Got This One Wrong. How Did It Happen? Donald Trump Intervened Personally to Install Jensen Huang at Nvidia. The Trump Put. The Whole Affairs. Better to Be Feared Than Loved. The Law of No Evidence. The War Against the Press. There’s Going to Be an Investigation. More on Chip Smuggling. The Market Roars. Morals Shmorals. The Lighter Side. I Got This One Wrong To state the obvious, I said this was not going to happen. I was wrong. One of the goals of this post is to explain my understanding, now, of why I was wrong. There were multiple things I got wrong. Most importantly, I did not understand how much Jensen Huang had set everything up to collapse like a house of cards without him. I did not expect the stock market to drop so far that a full Trump Put would be in play, where he would be willing to accept all the consequences of this action. I also expected the national security concerns to be more of a showstopper than they were. Others got this wrong too, or at least put this as unlikely, although I got it more wrong. Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday and then soared 31% on the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, which shows they did not expect it. What I continue to believe I was not wrong about was the essential actions of Jensen Huang, and that it is not acceptable for him to continue as CEO of Nvidia. This is a clear and present danger to national security. It is happening anyway, because, in a way I did not anticipate, not having Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia may be an even bigger danger. How Did It Happen? This was the Nvidia board announcement of Jensen Huang’s return. Nvidia Newsroom: NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it. The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries. Ryan Gould, Ian King, and Edward Ludlow (Bloomberg): “Thank you all for the second chance,” he said. “I am gonna be a better CEO the second time around.” For now Jensen Huang is being magnanimous, being thankful for the second chance and saying he was going to do better, and apologizing and saying he is going to therapy. We will see if that lasts. The board did not consult management, including the interim CEO. They got a call from Donald Trump, and then did what they had to do. The explanation is that now that they are satisfied that Jensen Huang being reinstated ‘poses no national security risk.’ As literally presented this is Obvious Nonsense. Of course Jensen Huang leading Nvidia poses a national security risk. What they mean is that Trump told them to do it anyway, that they would not be held responsible for that, and that not reinstating him would present both a national security risk and also a personal job security risk. The Editorial Board (WSJ): Mr. Trump claimed his Administration had conducted a “very thorough investigation” into Nvidia, and Mr. Huang was “exonerated.” That must be the quickest very thorough investigation in history. All of this suggests Mr. Trump assured the board that his Administration wouldn’t punish the company for possible violations of export controls or securities laws if they rehired the CEO. Later in the post I will examine exactly how much pressure was involved here. Donald Trump Intervened Personally to Install Jensen Huang at Nvidia At a high level, this is the story of The Fall and Rise of Jensen Huang. None of these facts is meaningfully in dispute: Jensen Huang and Nvidia sold a lot of chips to China, and sold a lot of chips to what are now known to be chip smuggling operations, and engaged in a systematic adversarial lobbying and technical compliance campaign while Jensen has a lot of affairs including with both a direct report and also one of the larger chip smugglers who is also an alleged spy according to government reports that know of the affair. The New York Times reports this information in public. Jensen Huang, under pressure and about to be fired, resigns from Nvidia. Nvidia stock tanks. Other stocks tank. Donald Trump personally calls for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. He ‘speaks to the board directly and indirectly’ on this matter. He makes it clear what he wants, and that he does not consider Jensen Huang a national security risk. The Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang, in a surprise move, without consulting management. It is very clear that step #4 was the key in causing step #5. Trump has said as much. I did not sufficiently seriously consider the possibility of #4 happening to this large an extent, or that it would be sufficient to trigger this style of intervention, and I predicted the national security state and others would fight back against it harder than they did. Aleph (November 18): The Jensen Huang affair is the first time I’ve ever seen NYC finance types be more clearpilled about a situation than tech people, which is interesting Samuel Hammond (November 19): Realism vs sycophancy. It was exactly the NYC finance types, rather than the San Francisco types or tech types, that made this happen, and that place such a high value on Jensen Huang, and that forced the President’s hand. The Trump Put Nvidia was judged, in this sense, Too Big to Fail (to have Jensen Huang as CEO). Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. Ryan Barber and Robbie Whelan (WSJ): The artificial-intelligence boom that had powered the U.S. stock market and economy for months was coming undone. Jensen Huang, the longtime CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia had been ousted following revelations of two affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Investors were hitting sell on the entire AI trade. President Trump told associates there was only one solution: getting Huang, a friend and ally, his job back. … What followed were a frantic 48 hours in which the president, the vice president and other top administration officials relayed [Attorney General Todd] Blanche’s assurances to board members as they rushed to rescue a leader Trump hadn’t even heard of when he began his second term. Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. items.title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
items.author: Stephen Clark
items.content: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks. The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001, and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history. Losing its voice The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate. Read full article Comments

items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
items.content: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster. It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I'm getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year.
